34024: The garden God planted "eastward in Eden", watered by a river that parted into the Pishon, Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates. The most common proposal places it in southern Mesopotamia near where the Tigris and Euphrates meet; alternatives include the Armenian highlands at the rivers' sources, the head of the Persian Gulf (now submerged), or a purely theological geography not meant to be mapped.
34028: The ark came to rest on "the mountains of Ararat", the biblical name for the kingdom of Urartu in the highlands of eastern Turkey and Armenia. The text names a region rather than a single peak; the point shown is the modern Mount Ararat, while older Syriac and Islamic traditions favoured Cudi Dagi (Mount Judi) farther south.
34029: Urartu is well attested in Assyrian inscriptions from the 9th to 7th centuries BC. Repeated claims of ark remains on Mount Ararat have not been substantiated by peer-reviewed work.
34032: The city and tower in the land of Shinar where human speech was confused and the peoples scattered. Babel is the Hebrew name of Babylon, and the tower is most often linked with a Mesopotamian ziggurat such as Etemenanki at Babylon; some scholars point instead to Eridu, an older city with a famous ziggurat.
34033: Foundations of Etemenanki, the great ziggurat of Marduk at Babylon, survive; ancient sources describe it as about 90 m square. Ziggurats were stepped temple-towers described as linking heaven and earth.
34036: Abraham's starting point, a major Sumerian city on the lower Euphrates. Most identify it with Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq; a minority argue for a northern Ur near Haran (for example near Urfa), noting the family's later ties to upper Mesopotamia.
34037: Leonard Woolley's excavations (1922-1934) uncovered the Royal Cemetery with its rich burials and the ziggurat of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100 BC), partly restored in modern times. The epithet "of the Chaldeans" reflects a later name for the region.
34040: A caravan city on the Balikh river in upper Mesopotamia where Terah's family settled and Terah died, and from which Abraham set out for Canaan. Jacob later fled to his uncle Laban here.
34041: Harran was a centre of the moon-god Sin; the Babylonian king Nabonidus restored its temple, and it was the last refuge of the Assyrian state after Nineveh fell (c. 610 BC). Ruins at Harran in southeastern Turkey include an early Islamic mosque and citadel.
34043: A city in the pass between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim where Abraham built his first altar in Canaan, Joshua renewed the covenant, and Israel rejected Rehoboam. Joseph's bones were buried here.
34044: Tell Balata, on the east side of modern Nablus, has Middle Bronze fortifications and a massive fortress-temple often linked with the temple of El-berith in Judg 9:46.
34049: Formerly Luz, renamed "house of God" by Jacob after his dream of the ladder. Jeroboam I later set up a golden calf here, making it a royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom condemned by Amos and Hosea. Most identify it with Beitin, north of Jerusalem; a minority favour el-Bireh.
34050: Excavations at Beitin (Albright and Kelso) found occupation through the Bronze and Iron Ages, though the sanctuary itself has not been located.
34054: A town east of Bethel where Israel was first defeated because of Achan's sin and then took the city by ambush. The usual identification is et-Tell; because et-Tell was unoccupied in the Late Bronze Age, others propose Khirbet el-Maqatir or Khirbet Nisya nearby.
34055: et-Tell was a large Early Bronze city abandoned around 2400 BC, with only a small Iron I village later. Khirbet el-Maqatir, excavated by the Associates for Biblical Research, has a small Late Bronze fortress argued by its excavators to be Joshua's Ai.
34059: An ancient hill city of Judah, earlier called Kiriath-arba, where Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah as a family tomb. Caleb received it as his inheritance, and David reigned here seven and a half years before moving to Jerusalem.
34060: The old city mound is Tel Rumeida, with Middle Bronze walls and an LMLK-era presence. The traditional Tomb of the Patriarchs is enclosed by a monumental Herodian wall that still stands.
34063: The grove near Hebron where Abraham camped, built an altar and received the three visitors who promised Isaac. The traditional site is Ramat el-Khalil north of Hebron.
34064: Ramat el-Khalil has a Herodian enclosure wall and the remains of a basilica built by Constantine after his mother-in-law reported pagan worship at the site.
34067: The "well of the oath" in the northern Negev where Abraham and Isaac made treaties over wells, and the traditional southern limit of Israel in the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba". Elijah fled through it on his way to Horeb.
34068: Tel Be'er Sheva, east of the modern city, preserves a planned Iron Age town with a deep well near the gate. Stones of a dismantled horned altar reused in a later wall are often linked with Hezekiah's reform.
34071: A town in the western Negev ruled by Abimelech, where both Abraham and Isaac passed off their wives as sisters and quarrelled over wells. Most identify it with Tel Haror on the Nahal Gerar; Tel Sera' is a less favoured alternative.
34073: One of the "cities of the plain" chosen by Lot and destroyed by fire and brimstone. The common proposal is the southeastern Dead Sea, linked with Early Bronze sites such as Bab edh-Dhra; a rival view identifies it with Tall el-Hammam north of the Dead Sea, and some think the site lies beneath the sea's southern basin.
34074: Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira show Early Bronze towns with large cemeteries that ended in destruction around 2350 BC. A 2021 paper proposing an airburst destruction at Tall el-Hammam drew strong criticism and corrections.
34076: The city of the priest-king Melchizedek, who blessed Abraham. Psalm 76 pairs Salem with Zion, and most Jewish and Christian interpreters identify it with Jerusalem; a minority link it to a Salem near Shechem.
34080: The "land of Moriah" where Abraham was told to offer Isaac. 2 Chronicles places Solomon's temple on Mount Moriah, so Jewish and Christian tradition identifies the site with the Temple Mount; Samaritan tradition places it on Mount Gerizim.
34081: The Temple Mount platform as seen today is largely Herod's expansion (from c. 20 BC); excavation on the platform itself is not permitted, but sifting of removed soil has recovered First and Second Temple period finds.
34084: The dry southern country of Judah, whose name means "dry" and came to mean "south". Abraham and Isaac grazed flocks here, and its seasonal streams gave the image of restoration in Psalm 126.
34085: Iron Age forts such as Arad and Tel Be'er Sheva and dozens of small fortresses dot the Negev highlands, alongside later Nabataean caravan towns.
34088: The Nile kingdom that repeatedly served as refuge and house of bondage: Abraham, Jacob's family and the infant Jesus all went down to Egypt, while Israel's exodus from it became the defining act of redemption in the Old Testament.
34089: Egyptian records mention "Israel" first on the Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC). The Beni Hasan tomb painting (c. 1890 BC) shows Asiatic travellers entering Egypt, illustrating the kind of migration described in Genesis.
34092: The pastureland in the eastern Nile Delta where Jacob's family settled and which was spared some of the plagues. It is usually located in the Wadi Tumilat and the surrounding eastern Delta.
34093: Tell el-Dab'a (ancient Avaris) in the eastern Delta shows a large population of West Semitic origin in the Middle Bronze Age, including Asiatic-style houses and burials.
34097: A store city built by Israelite forced labour and the starting point of the exodus. It is usually identified with Pi-Ramesses, the Delta capital of Ramesses II at Qantir; supporters of an early exodus date see the name as an update of an older place name.
34098: Magnetometry at Qantir has mapped a vast city of the 13th century BC adjoining the older site of Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a). Much of its stone was later carried to Tanis.
34102: The first stopping place of the exodus after leaving Rameses, in the Wadi Tumilat; the name is usually linked with Egyptian Tjeku. Not to be confused with Succoth east of the Jordan where Jacob built booths.
34105: The sea Israel crossed on dry ground while Pharaoh's army drowned. The Hebrew Yam Suph can mean "Sea of Reeds"; the point shown is the Bitter Lakes region on the isthmus of Suez, a common proposal, while others favour Lake Timsah, Lake Ballah, the Gulf of Suez, or the Gulf of Aqaba (where 1 Kgs 9:26 also uses Yam Suph).
34106: No archaeological remains of the crossing have been verified; claims of chariot wheels in the Gulf of Aqaba are not supported by scholarly study.
34108: The spring of bitter water, three days into the wilderness of Shur, that Moses made sweet by throwing in a piece of wood. The traditional identification is Ain Hawarah on the western Sinai coast; its location depends on the route and the crossing point assumed.
34110: An oasis with twelve springs and seventy palm trees where Israel camped after Marah. It is commonly placed at Wadi Gharandel in western Sinai, following the traditional southern route.
34112: The desert between Elim and Sinai where Israel grumbled for food and first received manna and quail. On the traditional route it is the coastal plain of el-Markha or the Debbet er-Ramleh in southwestern Sinai.
34115: The last camp before Sinai, where water came from the rock at Massah and Meribah and Israel defeated Amalek while Moses' hands were held up. It is traditionally located in Wadi Feiran or Wadi Refayid near Jebel Musa.
34120: The mountain where God gave the law and made covenant with Israel. Christian tradition since at least the 4th century identifies it with Jebel Musa in southern Sinai; alternatives include Jebel Serbal, Har Karkom in the Negev, Jebel Sin Bishar in western Sinai, and Jebel al-Lawz in northwest Arabia (in Midian, cf. Gal 4:25).
34121: St Catherine's Monastery at the foot of Jebel Musa was built under Justinian in the 6th century and holds one of the oldest continuously used libraries. No Late Bronze encampment has been identified at any proposed Sinai.
34125: The oasis in the wilderness of Zin from which the spies were sent and where Israel spent much of the wilderness period; Miriam died here and Moses struck the rock. It is usually identified with Ein el-Qudeirat, the richest spring in northeastern Sinai; Ein Qadis nearby preserves the name and is the main alternative.
34126: Tell el-Qudeirat has a sequence of Iron Age fortresses (10th to 6th centuries BC) but no Late Bronze remains, a key point in debates over the wilderness traditions.
34130: The summit in Moab from which Moses saw the promised land before he died; Deuteronomy says God buried him in a valley nearby and no one knows the grave. The traditional summit is Ras Siyagha, overlooking the Jordan valley and Jericho.
34131: Siyagha has a Byzantine monastery and church (4th to 6th centuries) with fine floor mosaics, visited by the pilgrim Egeria in the 380s.
34133: The plateau east of the Dead Sea between the Arnon and Zered gorges, home of Lot's descendants. Israel camped on the plains of Moab before entering Canaan, Ruth came from here, and its king Mesha rebelled against Israel.
34134: The Mesha Stele (found at Dhiban in 1868) records Mesha's revolt against the house of Omri, names Israel's God YHWH, and probably mentions the "house of David".
34137: The rugged land south of the Dead Sea, east of the Arabah, settled by Esau's descendants. Edom refused Israel passage, was subdued by David, and is denounced by Obadiah for gloating over Jerusalem's fall; later Edomites moved into southern Judah, which became Idumea, the homeland of Herod's family.
34138: Copper mining at Faynan and Timna peaked in the 10th century BC, showing a complex society earlier than once thought. Bozrah, Edom's capital, is Buseirah in southern Jordan.
34142: The kingdom of Lot's descendants on the upper Jabbok, with its capital at Rabbah (modern Amman). Its wars with Israel run from Jephthah to David's siege of Rabbah, during which Uriah was killed.
34143: The Amman Citadel inscription (9th century BC) is one of the few Ammonite texts. The Hellenistic and Roman city was called Philadelphia and belonged to the Decapolis.
34144: The homeland of the Midianites, usually placed in northwest Arabia east of the Gulf of Aqaba, though the people ranged widely as nomads. Moses fled here, married Zipporah and kept Jethro's flocks; later Midianite raiders were routed by Gideon.
34145: Qurayyah in northwest Saudi Arabia has a fortified settlement and distinctive painted pottery (late 2nd millennium BC), often called Midianite ware, also found at Timna.
34148: "The field of Aram", the region around Haran in upper Mesopotamia where Abraham's relatives stayed. Isaac's wife Rebekah came from here, and Jacob served Laban here for twenty years.
34150: The place by the Jabbok where Jacob wrestled through the night and was renamed Israel. Gideon later destroyed its tower, and Jeroboam I fortified it. It is often placed at Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sharqiyeh on the Jabbok, though this is not certain.
34153: A town on the trade route through northern Samaria where Joseph's brothers sold him to traders bound for Egypt. Centuries later the Arameans besieged Elisha here and his servant saw the hills full of fiery chariots.
34154: Tell Dothan, excavated by Joseph Free (1953-1964), was occupied in the Bronze and Iron Ages, with a large Late Bronze tomb complex.
34156: Israel's first camp west of the Jordan, where twelve stones were set up, the people were circumcised and the manna ceased. Saul was confirmed as king here, and later prophets condemned its worship. Its exact site east of Jericho is unknown; Khirbet el-Mafjar and several smaller sites have been proposed.
34160: An oasis city near the Jordan, the first city Israel took in Canaan when its walls fell. Elisha healed its spring, and in the Gospels Jesus healed Bartimaeus and called Zacchaeus there; the Good Samaritan's road ran from Jerusalem down to Jericho.
34161: Tell es-Sultan is among the oldest walled towns known, with a Neolithic stone tower (c. 8000 BC). Garstang dated a fallen wall to c. 1400 BC; Kenyon redated the city's destruction to c. 1550 BC; Bryant Wood argued for c. 1400 BC from pottery, and the dating remains debated. Herod's winter palaces lie about 2 km south at Tulul Abu el-Alayiq.
34164: Israel's central sanctuary in the time of the judges, where the tabernacle stood, Hannah prayed and Samuel grew up under Eli. After the ark was captured by the Philistines, Shiloh became a byword for a sanctuary God abandoned.
34165: Danish excavations (1920s-30s), Israel Finkelstein (1980s) and later teams found Iron I storage buildings and a destruction around the 11th century BC, consistent with the fall described in 1 Samuel and Jeremiah.
34170: A village in the hills south of Jerusalem, home of Ruth and Boaz and the birthplace of David. Micah foretold a ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah, and Matthew and Luke place Jesus' birth here.
34171: The Church of the Nativity was first built by Constantine (dedicated c. 339) over a cave venerated as the birthplace and rebuilt under Justinian. A clay bulla reading "Bethlehem" (7th century BC) was found in the City of David in 2012.
34175: A Benjaminite town notorious for the outrage against the Levite's concubine that sparked civil war, and later the home and capital of Saul. It is commonly identified with Tell el-Ful just north of Jerusalem; some argue for Jaba (Geba).
34176: Albright's excavations at Tell el-Ful found a small Iron Age fortress he called Saul's citadel; later re-examination has questioned that dating.
34180: Samuel's home, where he judged Israel and was buried. The Ramah of Benjamin is identified with er-Ram north of Jerusalem; whether Samuel's Ramathaim is the same place or lies farther northwest (for example at Rentis) is debated. Jeremiah's image of Rachel weeping in Ramah is cited by Matthew.
34183: A gathering place of the tribes where Samuel led national repentance and Saul was chosen king by lot. After Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, Gedaliah governed Judah from Mizpah until he was assassinated. Distinct from the Mizpah of Gilead in Gen 31:49.
34184: Tell en-Nasbeh shows a strong Iron Age wall and continued occupation in the 6th century BC, fitting its role as administrative centre after Jerusalem's destruction.
34187: One of the five Philistine cities and the home of Goliath. David feigned madness before its king Achish and later served him as a vassal at Ziklag. Hazael of Aram captured it in the late 9th century BC.
34188: Aren Maeir's excavations at Tell es-Safi found a large Iron Age city, an ostracon (2005) with names etymologically similar to Goliath, and a siege trench and destruction layer attributed to Hazael.
34191: A Philistine city where the captured ark was placed in Dagon's temple and the idol fell before it. Sargon II took Ashdod in 711 BC; in Acts Philip preached through Azotus after baptising the Ethiopian.
34192: Tel Ashdod (Dothan and Freedman) produced Philistine pottery and fragments of a Sargon II victory stele.
34194: The southernmost Philistine city on the coastal highway to Egypt. Samson carried off its gates and later died pulling down the temple of Dagon there; the road "down to Gaza" is where Philip met the Ethiopian official.
34197: A Philistine city that sent the ark back to Israel after plagues broke out. King Ahaziah of Israel later sent to enquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.
34198: A royal dedicatory inscription found at Tel Miqne in 1996 names Achish (Ikausu) son of Padi, kings of Ekron, confirming the site's identity; Padi is also named in Sennacherib's annals. The 7th-century city was a major olive-oil production centre.
34200: A Philistine seaport where Samson struck down thirty men. David's lament for Saul asks that the news not be told in its streets, and the prophets announced its ruin; Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it in 604 BC.
34201: The Leon Levy Expedition uncovered a Middle Bronze arched gate, a small silver-plated calf figurine, a Philistine cemetery (2016) and the 604 BC destruction layer. Ancient DNA from the site points to a southern European component in the early Philistine population.
34204: A border town in the Sorek valley where Samson married a Philistine woman and posed his riddle at the wedding feast. Tel Batash is the accepted identification; the Timnah of Judah in Gen 38 may be a different place in the hill country.
34207: A Danite town on a ridge above the Sorek valley, the home of Manoah and birthplace of Samson, who was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol. The Danites later sent scouts from here to find new land in the north.
34209: A ridge at the southeastern edge of the Jezreel valley where Saul and his sons, including Jonathan, fell in battle against the Philistines. David's lament curses its slopes for the fallen.
34212: A freshwater oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, with caves in the surrounding cliffs. David hid here from Saul and spared his life in a cave, cutting off only the corner of his robe.
34213: Finds include a Chalcolithic temple above the spring and a Byzantine-era synagogue whose mosaic inscription warns against revealing "the secret of the town", probably its balsam industry.
34216: A town in the Shephelah near whose caves David gathered about four hundred men in distress, in debt or discontented. Three of his mighty men broke through Philistine lines from here to bring him water from Bethlehem.
34218: The town Achish of Gath gave David as a base while he hid from Saul; Amalekites burned it and David recovered the captives. The point shown is Khirbet al-Ra'i, proposed by Garfinkel and Ganor in 2019; older proposals include Tel Sera' and Tel Halif.
34223: The Jebusite stronghold David captured and made his capital, where Solomon built the temple. Destroyed by Babylon in 586 BC and rebuilt after the exile, it was the scene of Jesus' death and resurrection and the birthplace of the church; the Romans destroyed it again in AD 70 and refounded it as Aelia Capitolina after 135.
34224: Hezekiah's tunnel carries the Gihon spring to the Pool of Siloam; its Hebrew inscription (found 1880) describes the two crews meeting. Other finds include the Broad Wall, the Stepped Stone Structure, bullae naming officials from Jeremiah, the Ketef Hinnom silver amulets with the priestly blessing, the Herodian Western Wall, and the Second Temple Pool of Siloam (uncovered 2004).
34227: The ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron. David climbed it weeping as he fled Absalom; Zechariah saw the Lord's feet standing on it; Jesus taught his disciples about the end from it, wept over the city on its slope, and ascended from it according to Acts.
34228: Its western slope has been a Jewish cemetery for millennia. Churches mark traditional sites, including the Eleona church built by Constantine and the Dominus Flevit chapel.
34231: The largest Canaanite city in the land, "head of all those kingdoms", which Joshua burned. Later Jabin of Hazor oppressed Israel in Deborah's day; Solomon fortified it and Tiglath-pileser III captured it in 732 BC.
34232: Yigael Yadin and Amnon Ben-Tor uncovered a massive Late Bronze city ended by fierce fire in the 13th century BC, a six-chambered gate attributed to Solomon (dating debated), and Akkadian cuneiform tablets.
34236: A fortress guarding the pass where the coastal highway enters the Jezreel valley, site of many battles. Solomon fortified it, Ahaziah died there, and King Josiah was killed there by Pharaoh Necho; Revelation's Armageddon is usually read as "mountain of Megiddo".
34237: Some 20 occupation layers include Canaanite temples, gates, water systems and pillared buildings debated as stables or storehouses. Thutmose III's account of his siege (c. 1457 BC) survives at Karnak. A seal reading "Shema servant of Jeroboam" came from here, and nearby at Kefar Othnay a 3rd-century prayer hall mosaic mentions "God Jesus Christ".
34240: A royal city of the Omride kings overlooking the valley that bears its name. Naboth's vineyard lay here, and Jehu killed Joram and had Jezebel thrown from a window here; Hosea named his son Jezreel as a sign of judgement on Jehu's bloodshed.
34241: Excavations revealed a large rectangular 9th-century enclosure with corner towers and a moat, typically linked with Ahab's dynasty, and a nearby winery.
34245: The hilltop capital Omri bought and built for the northern kingdom, where Ahab built a temple to Baal. It fell to Assyria in 722 BC; Herod rebuilt it as Sebaste. The name also came to mean the region between Judea and Galilee where Philip preached in Acts.
34246: Harvard and later excavations found the Omride royal acropolis, carved ivories (cf. Amos 6:4 and 1 Kgs 22:39), and the Samaria ostraca recording deliveries of oil and wine in the 8th century BC.
34249: The wooded ridge running to the Mediterranean at Haifa, a byword for fertility. Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal took place on it; the traditional spot is el-Muhraqa ("the burning") at the southeastern end overlooking the Kishon.
